newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions urge reforms as jobs debate revived.
newsitem.headline: German unions urge reforms as jobs debate revived.

text.p: Germany's top trade union at the weekend renewed calls for job creation through reforms in working practices as last week's news of record unemployment levels gave fresh impetus to the country's jobs debate.
The message came after Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) issued their second call in a week for a fresh jobs initiative involving the government, industry and unions.

In a commentary in the Volksstimme am Sonntag newspaper, the deputy director of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB) Ursula Engelen-Kefer urged companies to implement reforms which she said could create hundreds of thousands of jobs.

Cutting overtime hours by half would create 370,000 jobs, additional part-time work would creat 460,000 and a switch to a 35-hour week would take 570,000 people off the jobless lists, Engelen-Kefer said.
"The numbers prove it: unemployment can be fought, this cancer is no unavoidable fate," Engelen-Kefer said.

Meanwhile CDU general secretary Peter Hintze on Saturday spoke out in favour of new round table talks between employers, unions and the Bonn government following the news that German unemployment hit a post-war record of 4.16 million in December.
Hintze was echoing Kohl's call on Thursday for a return to broad negotiations on jobs. The chancellor described Germany's current jobless levels as "completely unacceptable."
"The co-operative culture that we have in Germany must be retained," Hintze told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper at the end of a two-day party leadership meeting.

Unions have so far given a lukewarm response to the idea of returning to talks with Bonn and employers, having quit Germany's so-called "alliance for jobs" last year in protest at the government's austerity plans.

The DGB's Engelen-Kefer said the union was "in principle" ready to enter broad talks on jobs, but said challenges to wage agreements by employers and an unsympathetic attitude by economics minister Guenter Rexrodt "does not exactly open the possibility of entering binding discussions."

In an interview with the Welt am Sonntag, Rexrodt denied that he did not take Germany's unemployment problem seriously, supported calls for cutting overtime and said the country must still aim to halve unemployment by the year 2000.
However he said it was not possible for Bonn to increase its spending to create new jobs, as trade unions are urging.

"Huge sums are already being spent on infrastructure in the new (eastern) states. No more is possible for budget reasons. Private investment is the decisive factor, and we are promoting this through our policies," Rexrodt said.
Meanwhile, a leading industrial representative poured cold water over the theory that fewer overtime hours would translate into more jobs, saying there was little scope for cuts.

Dieter Hundt, president of the German Federation of Employers' Associations (BDA), told German radio that overtime hours had already been halved in recent years, averaging at just 1.5 hours a week per worker in 1995.
However Hundt also said he still believed joblessness could be reduced by half by the year 2000 and urged politicians to continue to improve operating conditions for companies.
